opening_message:
Ticket 1: Haley Roberts (employee ID E021) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E021.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Haley Roberts (E021) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Source Code. As a full-time employee, write is within policy, and the Engineer role owns Source Code. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E021 (Haley Roberts) is a contractor with basic security training (HR note listed full-time, but security record says contractor). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Basic training => maximum is read. Requested write is above max, so recommend granting read.
reason: There is a conflict between the two notes: HR lists E021 as full-time Engineer (recommend write), while Security lists E021 as a contractor with basic security training (recommend read), based on a lookup in the security database. Under the contractor record, basic training allows at most read, and the requested write exceeds that maximum, so the grant is capped at read. Given the conflicting employment-type records, granting the lower, security-verified level (read) is the appropriate decision.

Let me work through this. The ticket asks for write access to Source Code for Haley Roberts (E021).

Team memory has two notes:
- HR note: role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommends write. Full-time Engineer owns Source Code, so admin would be allowed, write is fine → write.
- Security note: role Engineer (not verified), employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read. Contractor with basic training → max is read. Write requested, but above max → grant read.

Conflicting facts. The security note says security DB shows contractor while HR note says full-time. Which to trust?

The access policy distinguishes full_time vs contractor. The security agent looked up employment type in own database before writing, and looked up security training. HR note also looked up employment type in own database.

The conflict: HR says full-time, security says contractor. As the approver, I need to make a decision. The security note claims the HR note listed full-time but security record says contractor. Hmm.

Which record is more authoritative for employment type? Typically HR owns employment records. But the security agent also looked up in own database. The notes leave it ambiguous, but the security DB explicitly contradicts.

Given the conflicting info, the safer/least-privilege approach would be to grant the lower of the two recommendations: read. The policy says never grant more than requested, but request is write. The recommendations are write (HR) and read (Security). Security says contractor with basic training, so max is read. Granting read is consistent with the security record.

Given ambiguity, granting read is the conservative decision that satisfies both possible policies? If full-time Engineer, read is allowed (up to write requested, so they'd get write per policy). If contractor with basic training, read is max. The contradiction means we can't verify full-time status. 

I'll decide read, citing the security record showing contractor + basic training, making maximum read; requested write is above max, so grant read. Also note the conflict and that safety/least-privilege applies.

Let me submit.
